message.content: {"recommended_method":"social_choice","consensus_potential":0.58,"fairness_assessment":"A ranked or multi-criteria social-choice process is fairest because it compares access, expected usage, sustainability, and beneficiary needs rather than relying on the debate winner. Equal weighting should be reviewed if stakeholder groups have different levels of impact.","conflict_severity":"medium","stakeholder_analysis":[{"agent":"agent_1","position":"Favors option A: directing the full grant toward expanding the children’s book collection.","influence":0.32},{"agent":"agent_2","position":"Favors option B: creating a freely accessible digital space with computers; this position won the debate, but only with modest argumentative quality.","influence":0.36},{"agent":"agent_3","position":"Favors option C: splitting the grant equally between books and digital access, providing a compromise but potentially ignoring differing needs and costs.","influence":0.32}],"recommended_resolution":"collaborative","governance_reasoning":"The three options reflect legitimate but competing access priorities, and all have identified weaknesses. Use a participatory social-choice process with transparent criteria, stakeholder input, and ranked preferences; allow a conditional or phased compromise if evidence does not produce a decisive result. This is more robust than selecting the debate winner or imposing an equal split automatically."}
